title: Check if Matrix Is X-Matrix
spaceBreakdown:
- int n, i, j, onDiagonal: scalar locals → O(1)
- no containers, no recursion, no heap allocation
- not counted: input grid, returned bool
approach: Iterate over every cell (i, j) in the n×n grid. A cell lies on one of the two diagonals if and only if i == j (main diagonal) or i + j == n − 1 (anti-diagonal). For diagonal cells, verify the value is non-zero; for all other cells, verify the value is zero. Return false immediately on the first violation, otherwise true after the full scan. This is correct because the two conditions exactly partition the matrix into diagonal and non-diagonal cells, matching the problem definition.
hints: For a cell at row i and column j in an n×n grid, what two simple arithmetic relationships between i, j, and n tell you whether that cell sits on one of the two diagonals?
Use a single nested loop over the matrix. For cell (i, j) in Example 1 (n=4), cell (0, 3) satisfies i + j = 3 = n − 1, so it is on the anti-diagonal and its value 1 must be non-zero.

**Smallest valid input (n = 3)** - minimum matrix size, all diagonals non-zero, all others zero
`Input: [[1,0,1],[0,1,0],[1,0,1]]` → `Expected: true`
⚠️ Bug: using `i + j == n` instead of `i + j == n - 1` for the anti-diagonal → cell (0,2) with value 1 is treated as off-diagonal → returns false

**Zero on a diagonal cell** - a main-diagonal entry is zero
`Input: [[0,0,1],[0,1,0],[1,0,0]]` → `Expected: false`
⚠️ Bug: only checking off-diagonal cells are zero, skipping the non-zero check on diagonals → returns true

**AND instead of OR for diagonal test (even n)** - no cell lies on both diagonals when n is even
`Input: [[2,0,0,1],[0,3,1,0],[0,5,2,0],[4,0,0,2]]` → `Expected: true`
⚠️ Bug: using `i == j && i + j == n - 1` instead of `||` → no cell qualifies as diagonal, (0,0) = 2 treated as off-diagonal → returns false

**Non-zero off-diagonal element** - an off-diagonal cell has a non-zero value
`Input: [[5,7,0],[0,3,1],[0,5,0]]` → `Expected: false`
⚠️ Bug: only checking diagonal cells are non-zero, not checking off-diagonal cells are zero → returns true

followUps.q: The matrix is stored on disk in row-major order and you can only load one row into memory at a time. Can you still solve this?
followUps.a: Yes. The anti-diagonal test i + j == n − 1 only needs the current row index i and column index j, both available while scanning a single row. Load each row, scan its n elements, and apply the same checks. Time stays O(n²), space drops to O(n) for one row.

followUps.q: Instead of two diagonals, an X-Matrix is defined by k arbitrary lines through the grid, each given as a set of (row, col) coordinates. How does the approach change?
followUps.a: Build a boolean mask of size n×n marking every cell that lies on any of the k lines, then do the same single pass using the mask instead of the i == j or i + j == n − 1 test. Time is O(n² + total line cells), space is O(n²) for the mask.

followUps.q: Instead of returning true/false, return the minimum number of cells you must change to make the grid an X-Matrix.
followUps.a: During the same single pass, count diagonal cells that are zero (each needs one change) and off-diagonal cells that are non-zero (each needs one change). Return the sum. Time O(n²), space O(1).
